headline: Medium risk: shared networked automation can leak or misroute data, while prompt-injection and direct capability conflicts are limited by missing shared channels.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A (emqx) exposes only HTTP API/network egress, and agent B (social-auto-upload) has no filesystem read, MCP, browser, or shell path that would ingest A’s outputs by default. No shared communication channel is documented, so a prompt-injection bridge is not evidenced.
conditions: IF an orchestrator copies A’s HTTP responses into B’s prompt or config files, injection becomes possible.
IF a shared queue, clipboard, or filesystem bridge is added, B may parse attacker-controlled content.
mitigations: Keep A and B on separate accounts/workspaces.
Do not pipe A’s API output into B’s prompt text.
Disable any shared clipboard or message queue bridge.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging before any cross-agent handoff.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches IoT data and has broad network egress; B touches account data, images, and video content and also has broad network egress. Even without a shared filesystem, either agent can transmit its own context to external services, so a leakage pathway exists in default networked operation.
conditions: IF either agent receives sensitive IoT payloads or account data, that data can leave the local environment over network egress.
IF the operator places both agents under the same account or workspace, cross-exposure risk increases.
mitigations: Restrict outbound domains for both agents.
Run each agent under separate credentials.
Avoid feeding sensitive IoT or account data into either agent.
Review logs for accidental payload capture.
requires-engineering: add data-loss-prevention filters on outbound requests.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A has HTTP API access and broad network egress; B has broad network egress but no filesystem write, shell, subprocess, or git modification. Because B cannot write shared state and A’s write surfaces are not documented, direct capability conflict is limited and not shown to overlap.
conditions: IF an external orchestrator gives both agents write access to the same mutable resource, conflicts can emerge.
IF A is configured to mutate a shared HTTP-backed state store, contention may occur.
mitigations: Keep mutable resources single-writer.
Separate account files per B instance.
Avoid concurrent writes to any shared API target.
requires-engineering: add locking around shared state updates.

D_cascading_error.rationale: B’s social-media upload workflow can act on files and account data, while A can emit networked outputs from IoT-related workflows. If A’s outputs are forwarded into B without verification, B may publish or upload incorrect content; the pairwise handoff is plausible but not directly documented, so uncertainty pushes to medium.
conditions: IF A’s output is used as an input artifact for B, B may upload or publish it without independent verification.
IF the operator automates a pipeline from A to B, errors can cascade into external posts.
mitigations: Insert a human review step between A and B.
Validate A’s outputs before B consumes them.
Use a staging folder for B uploads.
Limit B to draft-only mode where available.
requires-engineering: add schema validation on A-to-B handoffs.

E_compliance.rationale: A touches IoT data and B touches account data, images, and video content, but neither profile documents residency, HIPAA, GDPR, or retention mismatches. With only docs-level evidence, compliance risk is present but not substantiated beyond generic cross-border/network handling.
conditions: IF regulated IoT telemetry or personal account data is processed under a jurisdictional policy, residency or retention mismatches may matter.
IF the operator routes EU PII or PHI through either agent, stricter controls are required.
mitigations: Confirm data-class handling before deployment.
Avoid regulated data until policies are documented.
Separate datasets by jurisdiction.
Review retention settings in both systems.
requires-engineering: document and enforce residency/retention controls.
